_meta.how_to_regress: npm run check:golden tool-finder  (dev backend up)
_meta.note: catalog parser quote-agnostic + categories array (was dropping 5 tools / [undefined]); max_tokens 2000. 2026-07-15: fixed a real bug — Tool Finder recommended itself as the top result (e.g. for 'Something broke and I don't know what to do'), which is always useless since the user is already using Tool Finder. Root cause: buildCatalog() fed the model its OWN entry (id 'ToolFinder') alongside every other tool, with no instruction to exclude it. Fixed by filtering 'ToolFinder' out of TOOL_CATALOG at build time (so the model never sees it as an option) plus a defensive second filter at response-validation time. GUARD: the vague-input case below MUST NOT return id:'ToolFinder' in recommendations — this is the single worst possible result and it doesn't require an exact wording match to check for, only its absence. 2026-07-15 (2nd pass, same day): fixed a second, more severe bug found while investigating the first — buildCatalog()'s field-extraction regex used a [^'"]+ character class that excludes BOTH quote characters even though tools.js only delimits a given string with ONE of them. Any title/tagline/description containing an apostrophe ('don't', 'it's', 'you're') got silently truncated mid-sentence right before it — 80 of ~121 catalog fields were affected. Example: BikeMedic's tagline is plain ('A trailside mechanic in your pocket', no apostrophe) but its fuller description ('...expert follow-up when standard repairs don't work') was being cut to '...standard repairs don' and, worse, catalogToString() only ever showed tagline OR description, never both — so BikeMedic's only catalog line shown to the model never mentioned bicycles at all. That's the direct cause of it claiming to cover 'bike, appliance, car, gear' for a vague query. Fixed: (1) new extractField() helper uses a backreference (['"]) ... \1 so only the ACTUAL opening delimiter closes the match, recovering full text for all 80 affected fields; (2) catalogToString() now joins tagline AND description when both exist and differ, so narrow tools have two chances to state their scope explicitly; (3) added an explicit anti-overreach rule to the system prompt (rule 8) as defense-in-depth even with fixed data. GUARD: the bike-scoped-hedge case below must contain 'bicycle' (or equivalent hedge) in BikeMedic's `why` for a vague query — the earlier bug produced 'physical object or mechanical item (bike, appliance, car, gear)' with no hedge at all. 2026-07-15 (3rd pass, same day): fixed the recommendation/no_perfect_fit boundary — rule 5 said to 'suggest which tool comes closest' without saying WHERE, so the model duplicated a wrong-domain tool into BOTH recommendations[] (which the frontend renders as a prominent 'Your best tool' card, singular header when length===1) AND no_perfect_fit (an honest caveat below it) — producing a contradictory UI: a big 'best tool' card for Bike Medic on a refrigerator query, with text underneath admitting it doesn't actually fit. Reproduced live: 'My refrigerator is not working right but I don't know what's wrong' returned BikeMedic as the sole card even after the scope-hedging fix (it was honestly hedged — 'While BikeMedic is designed for bicycles...' — but still shown as THE recommendation). Fixed by rewriting rule 5 and the no_perfect_fit schema description: true category gaps (no tool addresses the domain at all) must leave recommendations EMPTY and mention the closest tool only in no_perfect_fit prose, never both. Genuinely partial fits (e.g. CrisisPrioritizer/BrainDumpBuddy for the stress of something breaking) still populate recommendations normally — confirmed the fix didn't overcorrect into suppressing real partial matches. GUARD: the refrigerator case below must have an EMPTY recommendations array with BikeMedic mentioned only in no_perfect_fit.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: 2026-08-21: workflow -> order_note. The field is unchanged in purpose but the word was system vocabulary in a tool whose entire job is to remove system vocabulary; it renders under 'A useful order might be'. Output also stopped reading as search results: no match/relevance/percentage language, 'Start with X' as the heading, and 'When you get there:' on each card. 2026-08-21 (second pass): order_note and clarification REMOVED from the schema. Both sounded like sophisticated features and both gave the model room to overthink — the sequence contradicted 'I'd start with', and the generated question kept asking things that would help the RECOMMENDED tool rather than change WHICH tool. Replaced by a fixed, in-place correction box ('Not quite it? Tell me what's different') whose placeholder never goes stale. recommendations are capped at TWO in code.

input.problem: I have a huge messy list of unrelated small tasks and want to batch similar ones together to power through them

output.understanding: You have a bunch of unrelated small tasks scattered everywhere, and you want to group similar ones together so you can focus on one category at a time and move through them efficiently.

recommendations.title: Batch Flow
recommendations.why: BatchFlow groups your tasks into a schedule that works with your energy instead of fighting it — it takes your scattered list, organizes them by type, and builds a flow so you're not context-switching between unrelated work.
recommendations.what_to_do: Dump everything on your plate into it — the full messy list — and tell it what you're working with (time available, energy level, any tasks that have to happen in a specific order).

input.problem: Something broke and I don't know what to do

output.understanding: Something in your life stopped working and you're not sure where to start — whether it's figuring out what's actually broken, what it will cost to fix, or what your options are.

recommendations.title: Crisis Prioritizer
recommendations.why: This tool helps you separate what actually needs to happen right now from what can wait, which is the first question when something breaks. It can help you figure out whether you need an emergency fix today or whether you have time to research and plan.
recommendations.what_to_do: Tell it what broke and what concerns you most — whether it's safety, cost, how long you can live without it, or something else — and it will help you figure out what actually has to happen first.

output.no_perfect_fit: If the broken thing is a bicycle, Bike Medic can walk you through repairs step-by-step. If it's a plant, Plant Rescue can help diagnose and fix it. If it's clothing or a garment, Laundromat can help with rescue. If it's something else — an appliance, a car, a home system, or a device — there's no specialized tool in the catalog. Quote Check can help you evaluate whether a repair quote is fair if you get one. Otherwise, your next step is clarifying what broke so you can search for repair guidance or a local specialist.

input.problem: My bike chain keeps falling off

output.understanding: Your bike chain keeps falling off, and you need to figure out what's causing it and how to fix it.

recommendations.title: Bike Medic
recommendations.why: Bike Medic walks you through troubleshooting a chain that falls off—it can help you identify whether the problem is misalignment, wear, derailleur adjustment, or something else, and gives you step-by-step fixes you can do yourself or understand before taking it to a shop.
recommendations.what_to_do: Open it, describe what happens when the chain falls off (does it happen on certain gears, in certain conditions, or randomly), and tell it whether you've noticed anything else—noise, rubbing, how old the chain is.

input.problem: Something broke and I don't know what to do

output.understanding: Something in your life broke and you're not sure what the next step is — whether that's understanding what happened, figuring out who to call, or deciding what you can actually do about it.

recommendations.title: Crisis Prioritizer
recommendations.why: This tool helps you separate what actually needs to happen right now from what feels urgent because you're stressed. Tell it what broke and what you're worried about, and it will show you what genuinely requires immediate action versus what can wait — so you know where to focus first.
recommendations.what_to_do: Describe what broke, what you're concerned might happen if you don't act, and how much time you think you have. It will rank what actually matters by consequence, not by panic.

input.problem: My refrigerator is not working right but I don't know what's wrong.

output.understanding: Your refrigerator isn't working the way it should, but you're not sure what the actual problem is — whether it's not cooling, making noise, leaking, or something else entirely.

recommendations.title: Recipe Chaos Solver
recommendations.why: While Recipe Chaos Solver is built for cooking emergencies, it shares the same 'crisis in your kitchen, need to know what to do right now' structure. However, this is a partial fit — it's designed for mid-cook problems, not appliance diagnostics.
recommendations.what_to_do: Actually, this tool won't help with a refrigerator malfunction — it handles cooking and food prep issues, not appliance repair.

output.no_perfect_fit: The catalog doesn't include an appliance troubleshooting tool, which is what you actually need. You'd benefit from a tool that helps you diagnose what's wrong (is it temperature? noise? leaking?) and walks you through basic checks before calling a repair person, but that's not available here. Your best next step is to describe the specific symptom to a repair technician or search for refrigerator troubleshooting guides specific to your model — the more detail you can give (what you're noticing, when it started), the better they can help.
